# PART B — GP LETTER

```
20/05/2025

Dear Colleague,

Re: [Patient full name — not documented], DOB: not documented,
NHS No: not documented
Admitted: 19/05/2025, discharged: 20/05/2025 under Paediatrics
(specialty inferred — confirm).

This ten-month-old male (weight 9 kg) was admitted via GP referral with a
three-day history of coryza, worsening cough, noisy breathing, and poor
feeding, and was diagnosed with bronchiolitis.

On admission he had an RR of 58, SpO₂ of 90% on room air, mild-to-moderate
subcostal recession, and widespread fine crepitations and wheeze. He was
alert and not clinically dehydrated. A nasopharyngeal aspirate confirmed RSV.
He was managed supportively with supplemental oxygen (target SpO₂ ≥90%) and
nasogastric feeding. Antibiotics and salbutamol were appropriately withheld.
He improved steadily: oxygen was weaned overnight, NG feeds were removed as
oral intake recovered, and he was discharged on Day 2 tolerating full oral
feeds with SpO₂ 93–95% on room air and minimal work of breathing.

Diagnosis: Bronchiolitis (RSV-confirmed).

Medication changes: None — no medications on discharge.

Actions for you (GP): Not documented in the admitting notes.

Follow-up arranged: None. No routine follow-up was arranged at discharge.

Pending results: None.

Yours sincerely,
[Name, grade — to be completed by responsible clinician]
```

PART C - PATIENT VERSION (v2 second pass)

# Your Child's Discharge Letter

**This letter is for the parents and carers of your baby boy.**
It tells you what happened during his stay in hospital and what to do now.

---

## Why Your Baby Came Into Hospital

Your baby boy was brought in because he had been unwell for three days. He had a runny nose, a worsening cough, noisy breathing, and was not feeding well. He was also having fewer wet nappies than usual.

The doctors found he had **bronchiolitis** — a chest infection that affects babies. A test confirmed it was caused by a virus called **RSV (respiratory syncytial virus)**.

---

## What We Did to Help Him

When he arrived, the doctors checked his breathing and the level of oxygen in his blood. His oxygen level was a little low, so he was given **extra oxygen** through a small tube near his nose. As he got better overnight, the oxygen was slowly reduced and then stopped.

Because he was not feeding well enough, a small soft tube was passed through his nose into his stomach **(a nasogastric tube)** to give him milk feeds. As his feeding improved, the tube was removed. By the time he went home, he was feeding well by mouth.

He did **not** need any antibiotics or other medicines, because bronchiolitis is caused by a virus, not bacteria.

---

## Medicines to Take at Home

Your baby does **not** need any medicines at home.

---

## What Happens Next

No follow-up appointments have been arranged. If you have any concerns, please speak to your GP.

---

## When to Get Help

The doctors and nurses gave you safety-net advice before you left. Please follow that advice. If you are unsure what you were told, contact your GP or the ward to check.

If you become unwell or are worried about anything, contact your GP or call NHS 111. Call 999 if it is an emergency.

---

*This letter is a draft for review and sign-off by the responsible clinician before it is given to the family.*
